summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would adjust the Public Order legislation to accompany a new security framework for federal courts and tribunals in the companion Court Security Bill.
It would remove overlapping court provisions and refocus the remaining framework on prescribed investigatory authorities, including the Integrity Commissioner and Australian Crime Commission.
The substantive amendments would start with the new court security legislation, while the remaining authority-premises rules would distinguish public hearings from other proceedings.
changes: Specified Public Order offences would cease to cover Commonwealth premises used exclusively in connection with courts covered by the new framework.
A defendant relying on that court-premises exception would bear an evidential burden.
The existing Federal Court-specific provision would be repealed.
Rights to attend and remain for hearings at investigatory authority premises would be clarified as applying to public hearings.
summary.affected: Covered federal courts and tribunals, prescribed investigatory authorities and people attending their premises are affected.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Introduced the companion Court Security (Consequential Amendments) Bill, which removes overlapping provisions from the 1971 Public Order Act to allow the new Court Security Bill's framework to operate cleanly across federal courts and tribunals.

speeches.speaker: Michael Keenan
speeches.brief: Explained the Court Security Bill will replace the outdated Public Order Act with a modern framework giving trained security officers powers to search, screen and detain people at risk at Commonwealth courts including the Family Court of Western Australia and the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, with oversight from the Commonwealth Ombudsman.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Summed up the Court Security Bill, drawing on more than two decades practising family law to describe the stress, anger and hostility courts can see, and said the new powers for security and authorised court officers come with licensing, training and identification safeguards plus continued reliance on police for the most serious incidents.
